criteria: Ranked on the experience itself: what the attraction does to you in the seat, how much of it is built rather than projected, and how well it survives a fifth ride. Queue length, Lightning Lane tier and how hard something is to get on were deliberately ignored when setting the order — they are discussed in the prose, but they never moved a placement.
intro: Hollywood Studios is the strangest park at Walt Disney World to rank, because it only has nine actual rides. The rest of the roster is stage shows, walkthroughs, films and paid workshops. Any honest ranking has to mix those in rather than pretend the park is a ride park, so this list does — a 30-minute stunt show that has run since 1989 gets judged against a coaster on the same terms.

The other thing worth saying up front: this park's reputation is distorted by scarcity. Three of its attractions are among the hardest things to get on at the resort, and people reliably confuse difficulty with quality. Two of them earn the fuss. One of them does not, and it is ranked here where the ride deserves rather than where the queue implies.

ranking.headline: Four ride systems in eighteen minutes, and not one of them is the weak link.
why: The structure is what makes it. You are briefed in a rebel base, loaded into a troop transport, intercepted by a Star Destroyer, marched out into a hangar bay under two rows of stormtroopers, put into a trackless vehicle, chased through corridors, and finally dropped out the bottom of the ship. Most large Disney attractions have one good idea and stretch it across three minutes. This one changes its method four times and never loses the thread between them.

It is also the only attraction in the park where the money is visible. The hangar bay is the best sight line built in Florida this century, and it is a physical set rather than a screen. The tradeoffs are real and worth naming: it breaks down more than anything else here, it is the one ride sold as an individual Lightning Lane purchase instead of being included with Multi Pass, and standby regularly runs double the next-longest queue. None of that changes what happens once you are aboard. Minimum height is 40 inches.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if you are prone to motion sickness — the simulator segment and the closing drop both arrive fifteen minutes in, with no early exit.

ranking.headline: The best queue Disney has ever built, attached to a drop sequence that still won't tell you what's next.
why: Everything before the drop is the argument. The garden is overgrown on purpose, the lobby is dressed as if the guests walked out mid-drink in 1939, the boiler room corridor is genuinely unpleasant to stand in, and the library pre-show does its exposition in under two minutes without a single wasted line. By the time you are strapped into the service elevator you have been inside the story for ten minutes, which is why the first lurch upward lands harder here than on any other drop tower in the world.

The ride itself is a randomized sequence, so the number of drops and the order of the rises change between cycles. That is what keeps it re-rideable in a way that fixed-program drop towers are not — you cannot brace correctly because you do not know what is coming. It sits at 40 inches and is the most intense ride in the park for anyone who dislikes falling, well ahead of the coasters. Ride it at night if you can; the moment the doors open on the Sunset Boulevard view is better after dark.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if free-fall genuinely frightens you rather than thrills you — there is no gentle version of this and the drop is the whole point.

ranking.headline: Zero to highway speed in under three seconds, in the dark, with three inversions.
why: This is the only real thrill coaster at Walt Disney World with inversions, and the launch is still the best single moment of physical sensation in the park. The layout is unchanged from the original build: a linear-induction launch out of the loading bay, straight into a rollover, then a corkscrew, then a sustained dark run with almost no visual reference to tell you where the track is going. Riding without knowing the layout is a completely different experience from riding it for the fifth time, and it holds up either way because the forces are doing the work.

The Muppets retheme replaced the old rock-tour framing without touching the track, and that is the correct read on what people actually come for. The new material is funnier than what it replaced and the pre-show is a clear improvement, but nobody is queuing for the story. Two practical notes: at 48 inches it has the tallest height requirement in the park, and the ride is noticeably rougher in the back rows than the front, so if you have a bad neck ask for row one.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if you have back or neck problems — the launch and the transitions are abrupt and it is the roughest ride here.

ranking.headline: The best family dark ride in the park, and the rare headliner with no height requirement at all.
why: The trackless system is used well rather than just used. Vehicles split, converge, spin to redirect your attention and stall in the middle of a room so the gag lands where the designers want it — the salsa factory and the carnival room in particular do things a fixed-track ride physically cannot. The gag density is very high; the ride runs about five minutes and there is no dead space in it, which is more than most dark rides its size can claim.

The reason it is not higher is that it never risks anything. Every room is bright, cheerful and resolves within twenty seconds, and there is no equivalent to the hangar bay or the elevator drop — no moment where you stop reading it as a series of jokes. That is a defensible design choice for the one park headliner that anyone of any height can ride, and it is why this is the correct first ride of the day for a family with small children. It just means the ceiling is lower than the three above it.

ranking.headline: A carnival shooter with enough hidden scoring depth to survive a hundred rides.
why: The competitive hook is why this outranks several more expensive attractions. Every scene has high-value targets that only open if you hit a specific trigger first, so the gap between a casual player and someone who knows the ride is enormous — roughly a factor of three on the final score. That turns a five-minute family ride into something with a skill curve, and skill curves are the cheapest re-rideability a park can buy.

The physical execution helps: the vehicles spin to face each screen, the 3D is clean, and the spring-action shooters give real feedback instead of a plastic trigger. What holds it back is that it is entirely screens, and the pre-show and queue are thin compared with what surrounds them. Practically, it takes a lot of guests per hour and the queue moves faster than its posted time suggests, so a 45-minute board is often closer to 25.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if 3D glasses give you headaches, or if nobody in your party cares about a score.

ranking.headline: Thirty minutes of water, fire and boats that earns the seat you gave up an hour for.
why: The Hollywood Hills Amphitheater seats around 6,900 people and the show is built for that scale: water-screen projection across a full lagoon, live performers on a rockwork island, fire effects on the water, and a finale with a riverboat that reads as genuinely large. The best segments are the ones with physical staging rather than projection, and the sheer amount of water in play makes it a different category of spectacle from a fireworks show.

It is ranked here rather than higher because the middle sags. Several sequences run long, a couple of the projection segments have aged badly against the newer effects around them, and the show's structure is a loosely-connected clip reel more than a story. The bigger cost is time: getting a good seat means arriving well before the posted start, so the real commitment is closer to ninety minutes than thirty. It is worth it once per trip, not once per night.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if you are travelling with someone who cannot sit still for a long pre-show wait on a hard bench.

ranking.headline: The cockpit is the best set in the park; how good the ride is depends on your seat assignment.
why: The queue and the boarding are excellent — the full-scale ship outside, the crew lounge with the chess table, and then a cockpit built to the exact dimensions people have known for fifty years. Sitting down in it is the payoff, and it is a real payoff. The ride is a six-person cooperative simulator: two pilots, two gunners, two engineers, and the flight you get is genuinely determined by whether the pilots can steer.

The problem is that only two of the six jobs are interesting. Gunners press a button when a target appears; engineers press a button when a panel flashes. If you draw either, you are watching other people play a game, and the motion base is jerky enough that watching rather than driving makes the nausea worse. It is a headliner with a one-in-three chance of being the good version of itself, which is exactly why it sits below rides with no lottery in them. It is 38 inches, and the single rider line is usually the fastest way on — at the cost of any control over which seat you get.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if motion sickness is a concern and you cannot be guaranteed a pilot seat.

ranking.headline: A 1989 stunt show that still explains movie-making better than anything built since.
why: The framing is the thing that has kept it alive for nearly forty years: it stages an action sequence, stops, shows you the rigging and the safety mats, resets, and does it again for the cameras. You watch a stunt performer take a fall, and then you watch the crew explain how the fall was survivable. That is a documentary about craft disguised as a 30-minute show, and it is the only place in the park that does it.

The set pieces still land — the rolling boulder, the Cairo street with real fire, the plane. It is loud, the amphitheater is covered but not air-conditioned, and the audience-participation bit at the start goes on longer than it needs to. Most guests walk past this to queue an extra forty minutes for a ride, which is a bad trade. Go to a mid-afternoon performance, sit in the middle, and understand that the pacing is 1989 pacing — patient by modern standards, and better for it.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if loud pyrotechnics upset small children — the explosions are close and they are not subtle.

ranking.headline: A genuinely good family coaster carrying a reputation about two tiers above what it delivers.
why: Taken purely as a ride, it is well made. Two launches instead of a lift hill, a first drop with real airtime for a family coaster, a layout that runs over the top of the whole land so you get sight lines nobody else in Toy Story Land has, and a 38-inch requirement that lets most of a family on together. It is the best introduction to launch coasters in Florida for a nervous seven-year-old, and it is genuinely fun after dark when the lights come on.

But it is about two minutes long, it never exceeds moderate speed, and there is not a single element on it that you will still be thinking about at dinner. Its reputation comes from the fact that it is the hardest ride in this park to get on — often the first Lightning Lane return to sell out and routinely posting the longest Multi Pass wait in the park — and people rationalise a long wait by deciding what they waited for must have been extraordinary. It is a solid family coaster. Ranked on the ride, that is ninth here, and I would rather do the Indiana Jones show than queue an hour for it.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if you only have one park day and it would cost you your first two hours — there is no version of this ride worth that.

ranking.headline: Randomized scene combinations keep a 1989 simulator worth re-riding, if your stomach allows it.
why: The randomization is doing all the heavy lifting, and it works. Each flight assembles an opening, a planet, a hologram message and a destination from a large pool, so consecutive rides genuinely differ, and the roster has been expanded repeatedly over the years. That plus the queue — the droid workshop, the departure boards, the security scanner gag — makes this the most re-rideable thing in the park after Midway Mania.

The limits are the hardware. It is a screen in front of a motion base, and after Rise of the Resistance opened a hundred metres away the ceiling on that format is obvious. The motion is also aggressive relative to the visuals, which is a bad combination for anyone susceptible; this causes more sickness than anything else here. At 40 inches with a rider switch available, it is the ride most likely to split a family in half.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if simulators reliably make you queasy — this is the worst offender in the park for that.

ranking.headline: Twenty-five minutes of real singing under a roof, and the best seated rest in the park.
why: This is a condensed stage production of the 1991 film, and it is performed live rather than lip-synced, which puts it in a different category from most park stage shows. The ballroom sequence is properly staged, the costume work is good, and it runs 25 minutes, which is enough to feel like a show rather than a set piece. It has been running since the park's early years and the production values have been maintained rather than allowed to decay.

It is ranked here because it is a straight adaptation with nothing to say that the film did not — you are watching a very competent compression, not a reinterpretation. That is fine. Its practical value is high: the Theater of the Stars is covered, the benches are shaded, and slotting a performance into the early afternoon is the single best heat-management decision available on Sunset Boulevard.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if you do not like the film — the show adds nothing that would change your mind.

ranking.headline: The quietest room in the park, with original artwork and models almost nobody queues to see.
why: This is a self-paced museum of Walt Disney's career, and the artifacts in it are real: original concept art, a scale model of the Florida project as it was first pitched, awards, correspondence, and a working piece of early animation equipment. There is a short film at the end and usually a preview of whatever is in construction. You can walk it in fifteen minutes or spend forty-five, and no part of it moves you along on a schedule.

It sits at twelve because it asks something of you — if you are not interested in the history it is a series of glass cases. But the hit rate on people who try it is very high, and it is air-conditioned, effectively never busy, and the one place in this park where you can hear yourself think in the middle of the afternoon.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if nobody in your group cares how any of this was made.

ranking.headline: The best twenty minutes money can buy here, at a price that makes it a hard recommendation.
why: The build is a staged ceremony, not a retail transaction. The room is dark, a host runs the group through choosing one of four design themes, the parts are laid out on a moving belt, and the assembly ends with the hilt actually powering on in your hands. The staging is disciplined — no photography during the ceremony, no upselling in the room — and it produces something people keep for years rather than a souvenir cup.

It costs around $250 plus tax as of July 2026, and reservations are required and go quickly. That price is why it is ranked here rather than in the top ten: this is the one attraction on the list where I would tell most people the money is better spent elsewhere unless the person building it will genuinely care. If they will, it is the strongest memory the park sells.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if $250 is a meaningful amount of money on this trip, or if the recipient is unlikely to keep the thing.

ranking.headline: A free walkthrough with more real set dressing than most rides, and no line to get in.
why: It is nominally a shop, but it is built as an attraction: a full-size animatronic proprietor working behind the counter, shelves of aged props that were designed rather than bought, crates and jars with genuine backstory, and lighting that is committed enough to be dim. Ten minutes in here does more for the sense of place in Black Spire Outpost than either ride does.

The catch is obvious — the exit is a cash register, and the prices are steep. Go in with the intention of looking. It is ranked above several things with longer queues because it costs you nothing, takes ten minutes, and is one of the few places in the park where standing still is the point.

ranking.headline: Air conditioning, thirty minutes off your feet, and two hosts doing better work than the material.
why: The show works because the writing gives the two royal historians hosting it room to play, and the performers do — the between-song patter is genuinely funny and pitched over the heads of the children it is nominally for. The songs run with on-screen lyrics and the character appearances are brief and well-timed rather than dragged out.

As entertainment it is slight, and if you have no interest in the film it will feel like thirty minutes. As a scheduling tool in a park with almost no indoor seating it is close to essential: the Hyperion Theater is large, properly cold, and it can absorb the worst hour of the afternoon without a queue worth mentioning.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if nobody in your party wants to hear the songs — the comedy alone will not carry you through.

ranking.headline: Ninety seconds of pleasant whipping, with a queue that has never once been worth it.
why: It is a well-dressed flat ride: saucers on a whip mechanism under a canopy, the aliens overhead, a decent soundtrack, and at 32 inches it is the lowest height requirement in the park, so it is often the first ride a small child gets to do alone with a parent. The lateral snap when the saucer changes direction is genuinely more forceful than the visuals suggest.

That is the whole attraction. Ride time is roughly ninety seconds, the throughput is poor for a flat ride, and it routinely posts waits over half an hour because it is one of only three things in Toy Story Land. If it is under fifteen minutes, ride it. If it is not, walk on. Nothing in it changes on a second ride.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if the posted wait is above fifteen minutes and you have anything else left to do.

ranking.headline: A build-your-own workshop that is more toy store than attraction, but the toy actually works.
why: You pick parts off a conveyor belt, assemble a unit at a bench in about fifteen minutes, and leave with a remote-controlled droid that responds to beacons planted around Galaxy's Edge — which is the part people underrate, because the droid keeps doing things for the rest of the day rather than sitting in a bag. Staff help without taking over, and the choice between the two chassis types is a real choice.

It ranks below Savi's because the ceremony is not there: it is a bench, a belt and a build, closer to a retail experience with a theme than a staged one. It is also expensive, and the droid is fragile enough that it wants careful packing. Worth it for a child who will play with it at home; skippable for anyone who wants the moment more than the object.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if you are not buying — unlike Dok-Ondar's, there is nothing here to look at.

ranking.headline: Props, replicas and short character lines in an air-conditioned hall almost nobody walks into.
why: It is an exhibition space: film props and replicas, production material, a short behind-the-scenes film, and character greetings at the back with queues that are usually a fraction of what the same characters draw elsewhere. On a hot afternoon it is the fastest character meet in the park and one of the easiest places to disappear into for twenty minutes.

It is last on this list because it is a holding room with good contents rather than a designed experience, and it has been visibly overtaken by what Galaxy's Edge does across the park. But it is free, indoor and empty, and those three things together are rarer here than they should be.
ranking.skipIf: Skip it if you have already done Galaxy's Edge properly — this will feel like a smaller version of it.

overrated.why: Ranked ninth above and still overrated — that is the point. It is a good family coaster with bad queue economics: routinely the longest Multi Pass wait in the park and the first return window to disappear, for a two-minute ride with no standout element. The scarcity is doing the reputational work, not the layout.

Four of the six seats are button-pressing jobs, and the ride sells itself on a cockpit you experience for about four minutes. Ranked seventh because the pilot version is very good, but most guests never draw it and are quietly disappointed without being able to say why.

Ninety seconds of ride behind a queue that regularly exceeds thirty minutes. It is a competent flat ride carried entirely by being one of three attractions in a land that draws far more people than it can process.

underrated.why: It has been running since 1989 and is written off as an old show, which is exactly backwards — it is the only attraction at Walt Disney World that stops mid-sequence to show you the rigging, and the fire effects are still bigger than anything else on stage here.

Original artwork, the original Florida project model and a genuinely quiet room, with effectively no wait at any hour. Most guests walk past the door without registering that it is an attraction at all.
A full-size animatronic proprietor and a room of purpose-built props, free to walk into, no queue, and better set dressing than plenty of things people wait an hour for two hundred metres away.

The randomization means the ride you get today may share nothing with the one you rode last trip, which almost nobody accounts for when they say they have already done it. It is the second most re-rideable attraction in the park.

faqs.q: What is the single best ride at Hollywood Studios?
faqs.a: Star Wars: Rise of the Resistance, and it is not a close call. It runs about eighteen minutes across four different ride systems, and the hangar bay set is the most impressive physical space Disney has built in Florida in decades. The caveats are that it breaks down more than anything else in the park and that it is sold as a separate Lightning Lane purchase rather than being included with Multi Pass.

faqs.q: What should I ride first at rope drop?
faqs.a: Slinky Dog Dash or Rise of the Resistance, depending on what you have bought. If you are paying for Rise separately, go to Slinky Dog Dash at opening, because it is the ride whose standby wait deteriorates fastest and the one that is hardest to fix later in the day. If you are not paying, walk straight to Rise and take the shortest standby line it will ever have.

faqs.q: How many actual rides does this park have?
faqs.a: Nine: Rise of the Resistance, Millennium Falcon: Smugglers Run, Slinky Dog Dash, Toy Story Midway Mania, Alien Swirling Saucers, Tower of Terror, Rock 'n' Roller Coaster, Star Tours and Mickey & Minnie's Runaway Railway. Everything else is a show, a walkthrough, a film or a paid workshop. Plan for a park where sitting down in a theater is a normal part of the day rather than a fallback.

Alien Swirling Saucers is 32 inches, Slinky Dog Dash and Millennium Falcon: Smugglers Run are 38, Star Tours, Rise of the Resistance and Tower of Terror are 40, and Rock 'n' Roller Coaster is 48 — the tallest requirement in the park. Runaway Railway and Toy Story Midway Mania have no requirement at all, which makes them the two headliners a whole family can do together. Rider switch is available on most of the rest.

faqs.q: Is one day enough for Hollywood Studios?
faqs.a: One long day covers the nine rides and two or three of the shows if you arrive at opening and stay to close. It is not enough to do Galaxy's Edge at walking pace, see Fantasmic and eat a sit-down meal. If you only have one day, decide in advance whether you are prioritising rides or Galaxy's Edge itself, because trying to do both properly is the most common way people leave this park frustrated.
